answer_text:
Let

\[
z_k=2\pi i k,\qquad k\in\mathbb Z,\ k\neq 0,
\]

and write

\[
f(z)=\frac{z}{(1-e^z)\sin z}.
\]

We check the order of the zero of the denominator at \(z_k\).

First,

\[
e^{z_k}=e^{2\pi i k}=1,
\]

so

\[
1-e^{z_k}=0.
\]

The function \(g(z)=1-e^z\) has derivative

\[
g'(z)=-e^z.
\]

Thus

\[
g'(z_k)=-e^{2\pi i k}=-1\neq 0.
\]

Therefore \(1-e^z\) has a simple zero at \(z=z_k\).

Next, check the sine factor:

\[
\sin z_k=\sin(2\pi i k)=i\sinh(2\pi k).
\]

Since \(k\neq 0\), \(\sinh(2\pi k)\neq 0\), so

\[
\sin z_k\neq 0.
\]

Hence the denominator \((1-e^z)\sin z\) has a simple zero at \(z=z_k\).

Finally, the numerator is

\[
z_k=2\pi i k\neq 0,
\]

so there is no cancellation.

Therefore \(f\) has a simple pole at each \(z=2\pi i k\), \(k\neq 0\). The order of each such pole is

\[
\boxed{1}
\]
